**Surat al-Hashr (The Gathering)**

Medinan, and its verses number twenty-four.

﴿Whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth glorifies Allah, and He is the Mighty, the Wise.﴾ What has been said about this in the opening of Surat al-Hadid has already passed. The relative pronoun is repeated here to emphasize and draw attention to the independence of each of the two groups in glorifying Allah. It is narrated that when the Prophet, upon him be blessings and peace, arrived in Medina, he made a treaty with Banu al-Nadir, who were a group of Jews descended from Harun, peace be upon him. They had settled in Medina during the trials of the Children of Israel, awaiting the mission of the Prophet, upon him be blessings and peace. He made a covenant with them that they would be neither with him nor against him. When he, upon him be blessings and peace, prevailed on the day of Badr, they said: "This is the Prophet whose description is in the Torah; his banner will never be turned back." But when the day of Uhud came and what happened happened, they doubted and broke the covenant. Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf set out with forty riders to Mecca, and they allied with the Quraysh at the Ka'bah against him, upon him be blessings and peace. The Prophet, upon him be blessings and peace, then commanded Muhammad ibn Maslamah al-Ansari, who killed Ka'b by treachery; Ka'b had been his foster-brother. Then he attacked them at dawn with the army, and said to them: "Leave Medina." They asked him, upon him be blessings and peace, for a delay of ten days so that they might prepare for departure. Abd Allah ibn Ubayy the hypocrite and his companions secretly sent word to them: "Do not leave the fortress. If they fight you, we are with you and will not abandon you; and if you leave, we will certainly leave with you." So they fortified the alleys and barricaded them. The Prophet, upon him be blessings and peace, besieged them for twenty-one nights. When Allah cast terror into their hearts and they despaired of the support of the hypocrites, they sought peace. He refused them anything except exile, on condition that each three of them could carry on one camel whatever goods they wished. They departed for Syria, to Jericho and Adhri'at, except for two households of them, the family of Abu al-Huqayq and the family of Huyayy ibn Akhtab, who joined Khaybar. A group of them joined al-Hirah. Then Allah the Exalted revealed ﴿Whatever is in the heavens glorifies Allah﴾ up to His words: ﴿And Allah is over all things capable.﴾

(p-225)

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 59, verse 2:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿It is He who expelled those who disbelieved among the People of the Book from their homes﴾ is an explanation of some of the effects of His might (ʿizzah) and the rulings of His wisdom (ḥikmah), following His description, exalted is He, with overpowering might and dazzling wisdom absolutely. The pronoun refers to Him, exalted is He, under that title, either on the basis that the attribution of these two qualities to Him is fully manifest, with complete support from the context, or by treating it as a substitute for the demonstrative (ism al-ishārah), as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say: Have you considered, if Allah took away your hearing and your sight and sealed over your hearts, what god other than Allah could restore them to you?﴾, meaning: "by that." On this is the saying of Ru'bah ibn al-'Ajjaj:

؎ [As if on the skin were the spreading of leprosy (bahaq)]

as is well known. It is as if it were said: "That One described with might and wisdom, who expelled ...etc." In this there is an indication that in the expulsion there is dazzling wisdom. His saying, exalted is He: ﴿at the first gathering﴾ means: at the first of their gathering (ḥashr) to Syria. They were from a tribe that had never been struck by exile (jalā') before, and they were the first to be expelled from the Arabian Peninsula (Jazirat al-'Arab) to Syria. Or this was the first of their gathering. The last of their gathering was the exile by ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with him, of them from Khaybar to Syria. It is also said: the last of their gathering is the gathering of the Day of Resurrection, because the place of assembly (mahshar) will be in Syria.

﴿You did not think﴾ O Muslims,

﴿that they would leave﴾ their homes in this humiliation and disgrace, because of the strength of their might and the power of their defences.

﴿And they thought that their fortresses would protect them from Allah﴾ means: they thought that their fortresses would prevent them, or that they would be a barrier for them from the might of Allah, exalted is He. The change of structure, by placing the predicate first and attributing the clause to their pronoun, is to indicate the completeness of their confidence in the impregnability of their fortresses and their belief in themselves that they were in a state of might and protection, such that they cared nothing for anyone who might confront them or covet their dominance. It is permissible that "mani'atuhum" be the predicate of "anna," and "ḥuṣūnuhum" be raised as the subject.

﴿So Allah came upon them﴾ meaning: the command of Allah, exalted is He, and His decree destined for them.

﴿from where they did not expect﴾ and it did not occur to their minds, and that was the killing of their chief Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf, for it (p-226) was among what weakened their strength, dispersed their power, and stripped their hearts of security and tranquillity. It is also said: the pronoun in "atahum" and "lam yahtasibu" refers to the believers, meaning: the help of Allah came to them. It is read "fa-ātāhum," meaning: Allah brought them the punishment or the victory.

﴿And He cast terror into their hearts﴾ meaning: He established in them the fear that terrifies them, that is, fills them.

﴿They destroyed their houses with their own hands﴾ in order to block the mouths of the alleys with what they tore from them of wood and stones, and so that no dwellings would remain for the Muslims after their exile, and so that they might carry with them some of their desirable fittings that are transportable.

﴿and with the hands of the believers﴾ where they were destroying them to remove their strongholds and places of defence, and to widen the field of battle, and as a vexation to them. The attribution of this to them is because they were the cause of it, as if they had burdened them with it and commanded them to do it. It is said: the clause is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) or an explanation of "terror." It is read "yukharribūna" with doubling for intensification. It is also said: al-ikhrāb means rendering something desolate or leaving it in ruin, while al-takhrīb means tearing down and demolishing.

﴿So take warning, O people of insight﴾ be admonished by what befell them of terrible matters, in a manner that minds scarcely reach, and guard against engaging in the disbelief and sins that led them to it; or pass from the state of the two groups to the state of yourselves, so do not rely on the mutual support of means, but put your trust in Allah, mighty and majestic. It has been used as evidence for the authority of analogy (qiyas), as explained in its proper place.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 59, verse 3:

﴿And had it not been that Allah had decreed for them the exile﴾, i.e., the departure from their homelands in that dreadful manner.

﴿He would have punished them in this world﴾ by killing and captivity, as was done to the Banu Qurayza.

﴿And for them in the Hereafter is the punishment of the Fire﴾. This is a resumptive clause (isti'naf) not connected to the response (jawab) of "law la" (had it not been). It was brought to explain that, although they were spared the punishment of this world by the decree of exile, there is no escape for them from the punishment of the Hereafter.

**﴿That﴾**, i.e., what befell them and what will yet befall them.

**﴿Because they opposed God and His Messenger﴾**, by reason of their having done what they did of the vile deeds reported of them.

**﴿And whoever opposes God﴾** — it is also read "yushāqiq Allāh" (﴿yushāqiqi Allāha﴾), as in Surat al-Anfal. The restriction to mention of opposing God Most High is because it entails opposing him (ﷺ) as well, and to match the words of God Most High: **﴿for God is severe in punishment﴾**. This [clause] is either the consequent itself, with the returning pronoun (al-ʿāʾid) to "man" omitted according to those who require it, i.e., "severe in punishment for him"; or it is a causal justification for the omitted consequent, i.e., "God will punish him, for God is severe in punishment." In either case, the conditional sentence completes what precedes it, confirms its meaning, and establishes the causal link by way of demonstrative proof, as if it were said: that which has befallen them of punishment, both hastened and deferred, is due to their opposing God Most High and His Messenger; and everyone who opposes God, whoever he may be, has for that reason a severe punishment; so for them there is indeed a severe punishment.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 59, verse 5:

﴿Whatever palm trees you cut down﴾, i.e., whatever palm tree (nakhla) you cut down. The word is "li'na" (lina), a form of the pattern "fi'la" derived from the root l-w-n, and its "ya'" is substituted for an original "waw" because of the kasra preceding it, as in "dima" (dima, from dawma). It is pluralized as "alwan" (alwan). It has also been said that it derives from "al-lin" (softness), in which case its plural is "liyan" (liyan), and it refers to the noble palm tree (al-nakhla al-karima).

﴿Or you left them﴾: the pronoun refers to "ma" (whatever), and its feminine form is due to its being explained by "al-lina" (the palm tree), as in the words of God Most High: ﴿Whatever mercy Allah opens to people, none can withhold it﴾.

﴿Standing upon their roots﴾, just as they were, without you having touched them in any way. It has been read as "ala usulihā" (ala usulha), with the "waw" of "usul" dropped, either by elision (al-iktifa') with a damma, or on the basis that it is a plural like "rukhun." It has also been read as "qa'iman" (qa'iman) on "usulihi" (usulihi), taking "ma" in its literal sense.

﴿So by the permission of Allah﴾: that is, its cutting and its leaving were by the command of Allah Most High.

﴿And so that He might disgrace the defiant ones﴾: i.e., and so that He might humiliate the Jews and enrage them by this permission to cut and to leave. For when they see the believers disposing of their property as they wish, and acting with it as they choose, cutting or leaving, their rage increases and their regret is multiplied. From this it has been derived that it is permissible to demolish the abodes of the disbelievers, cut down their trees, and burn their crops in order to increase their rage. The singling out of the lina for cutting, if it is from the "alwan" category, is so that the 'ajwa and the barniyya (two noble varieties of palm) are preserved, since they are the noblest of palms; and if the lina is itself the noble variety, then the purpose is to make their rage more intense.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 59, verse 6:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And what Allah restored to His Messenger from them﴾ is the beginning of an explanation of the state of what was taken from their wealth, after the explanation of what befell their persons of immediate and deferred punishment, and what was done to their homes and palm trees of destruction and cutting down. That is, what He returned to him (ﷺ) of their property. In this is an indication that he was worthy of having it, and that it had fallen into their hands without right, so Allah, Exalted is He, returned it to its rightful owner, because Allah, Exalted is He, created people to worship Him, and created what He created so that they might use it as a means to His obedience. Thus it is fitting that it belong to the obedient.

﴿From them﴾ meaning: from the Banu al-Nadir.

﴿You did not press forward against it﴾ meaning: you did not make any hurried advance to obtain and seize it, from the wajif, which is rapid travel.

﴿With horses or camels﴾: the rikab is what is ridden of camels specifically, just as the rakib (rider) among them is one who rides a camel and no other. As for one who rides a horse, they call him a fāris (horseman), and it has no singular from its own word; its singular is rāḥilah. The meaning is: you did not traverse a great distance for it, nor did you encounter severe hardship, nor fierce fighting. This is because their villages were two miles from Medina, so they walked to them on foot, and there was no rider among them except the Prophet (ﷺ). He conquered them by agreement, without any race taking place between them. It is as if it were said: "And what Allah restored to His Messenger from them, you did not acquire it by the toil of the right hand and the sweat of the brow."

﴿But Allah gives His messengers power over whomever He wills﴾: that is, His custom, Exalted is He, is to empower them over whichever of their enemies He wills, with a special empowerment. He empowered the Prophet (ﷺ) over these people with an empowerment that was not customary, without you having to plunge into the narrow passes of calamities or endure the severe hardships of wars. Therefore you have no right to their property.

﴿And Allah is over all things competent﴾: so He does what He wills as He wills, sometimes in the known manners and sometimes in other than them.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 59, verse 7:

The words of Allah, Exalted: ﴿What Allah has bestowed upon His Messenger from the people of the towns﴾ are an explanation of the channels of fay' (fay', spoils acquired without fighting) after the explanation of its being bestowed upon him, peace and blessings be upon him, without the fighters having any right in it. The repetition of the same phrase of the first statement is for emphasis, and the placing of "the people of the towns" in the position of their pronoun is to indicate that what is [bestowed] includes their estates as well.

﴿So it belongs to Allah, and to the Messenger, and to the near relatives, and the orphans, and the needy, and the wayfarer﴾. Scholars have differed concerning the division of fay'. It has been said: it is divided into six parts, according to the apparent meaning of the verse, and the share of Allah is spent on the Ka'bah and the rest of the mosques. It has also been said: it is divided into five parts, like the spoils of war (ghanimah), because the mention of Allah is for glorification, and the share of the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, is now spent on the imam according to one opinion, on the armies and frontier garrisons according to another, and on the public interests of the Muslims according to a third. It has also been said: it is divided into five parts like the spoils of war, for he, peace and blessings be upon him, used to divide the fifth in this manner and would spend the four-fifths as he wished, and now [the matter stands] according to the disagreement mentioned.

﴿So that it does not become⁠﴾, that is: the fay' which by right should belong to the poor, who live by it.

﴿a circulating commodity (dulah)⁠﴾, with a dammah on the dal, and it has been read with a fatha. It is that which circulates for a person, that is, which turns over between wealth, fortune and dominance. It has also been said: dawlah with a fatha means [from] sovereignty (mulk) with a kasrah, or with a dammah in wealth and with a fatha in victory; that is: so that it does not become mere fortune.

﴿among the rich among you⁠﴾, who multiply by it. Or: so that it does not become a jahili (pre-Islamic) circulation among you, for the chiefs among them used to monopolize the spoils and would say: "Whoever is mighty takes the plunder." It has also been said: dulah with a dammah is what is passed around, like ghurfah, the name of what is scooped up. The meaning then is: so that fay' does not become something the rich pass around among themselves and take turns with, so that it does not reach the poor. And dawlah with a fatha means circulation. The meaning then is: so that it does not become something circulating among them, or so that their holding it does not become a circulation among them, not bringing it out to the poor. It has also been read as "dawlatun" with a raf', taking "kana" as complete, meaning: so that there does not occur a circulation according to the meanings detailed.

﴿And whatever the Messenger gives you⁠﴾, that is: whatever he has given you of the fay', or of the command.

﴿take it⁠﴾, for it is your right, or hold fast to it, for it is obligatory upon you.

﴿And whatever he forbids you from⁠﴾, from taking it or from engaging in it.

﴿refrain⁠﴾ from it.

﴿And fear Allah⁠﴾ by opposing him, peace and blessings be upon him.

﴿Indeed, Allah is severe in punishment⁠﴾, so He punishes whoever opposes His command and His prohibition.

﴿For the poor emigrants﴾ is a substitute (badal) for ﴿to the near of kin﴾ and what is joined to it. The Messenger, peace be upon him, is not called poor, and whoever gives to the wealthy near of kin has specified the substitution by what follows it. As for restricting the consideration of poverty to the fay' (spoils returned to the Muslim community without battle) of the Banu al-Nadir, it is a manifest distortion.

﴿Who were expelled from their homes and their possessions﴾, where the disbelievers of Makkah compelled them and forced them to leave, and they were a hundred men, and they went out from it.

﴿Seeking bounty from Allah and His good pleasure﴾, i.e., seeking from Him, exalted is He, provision in this world and approval in the Hereafter. They were first described with what indicates their entitlement to the fay', namely their expulsion from their homes and possessions, and this was then qualified secondly by what makes their status great and confirms it.

﴿And they help Allah and His Messenger﴾ is conjoined to "seeking" (yabtaghun), so it is either a circumstantial clause anticipated (ḥāl muqaddara), meaning intending to support Allah, exalted is He, and His Messenger, or a concomitant circumstance (ḥāl muqārina), for their departure from among the disbelievers, defying them, emigrating to Madinah, is support. And what support it is!

﴿Those﴾ are the ones described by the praiseworthy qualities detailed above.

﴿They are the truthful﴾, the firmly established in truthfulness, as this became manifestly evident through what they did.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 59, verse 9:

﴿And those who had settled (tabawwa'u) the abode and the faith﴾ is a resumptive statement (kalam mustanaf) brought in to praise the Helpers (al-Ansar) for commendable qualities, among which is their love for the Emigrants (al-Muhajirin) and their contentment at the exclusive allocation of the spoils (fay') to them, with the best and most complete contentment. The meaning of their settling (tabawwu') the abode is that they took Madinah, and the faith, as a dwelling-place (mabaah), and they established themselves in both with the utmost firmness, by treating the state as if it were a place. It has been said: tabawwu' was given the meaning of adhering (luzum). It has been said: they settled the abode and sincerely held the faith, like the saying of the one who said: [I fed her straw and cold water]. It has been said: the meaning is that they settled the abode of emigration and the abode of faith, so the second term of the first was omitted and replaced by the definite article (al-lam). It has been said: he named Madinah "faith" because it is its manifestation (mazhar) and its origin (mansha').

﴿from before them﴾ means: before the emigration of the Emigrants according to the first meanings, and before the settling of the Emigrants according to the last two. It is permissible to take the adoption of the faith as a dwelling-place, its adherence and its sincere holding, according to the first meanings, as an expression for the establishment of all its rights, of which is the manifestation of all its rites and rulings. There is no doubt about the precedence of the Helpers in this over the Emigrants, because the Emigrants were incapable of manifesting some of them, not in their sincerity of heart and conviction, since their precedence over them in that is inconceivable.

﴿They love those who emigrate to them﴾ is a predicate of the relative pronoun (khabar lil-mawsul), meaning: they love them insofar as they emigrated to them, because of their love of the faith.

﴿and they find in their breasts﴾ means: in their souls.

﴿any need (hajah)﴾ means: something they need. It is said: take from him your need (hajah), meaning what you require. It has been said: it means a trace of a need, such as craving, envy, or rage.

﴿of what they have been given﴾ means: of what the Emigrants were given of the fay' and other things.

﴿and they prefer﴾ means: they give precedence to the Emigrants.

﴿over themselves﴾ in every matter of the means of livelihood, to the extent that whoever had two wives would step down from one of them and marry her to one of them.

﴿even though they themselves were in need (khasasah)﴾ means: poverty and want; its origin is the gaps (khasas) of the house, which are its openings. The clause is in the position of a circumstantial phrase (hal), and you have known its aspect many times. "The Prophet (ﷺ) divided the wealth of the Banu al-Nadir among the Emigrants and did not give the Helpers anything except three needy men: Abu Dujanah Simak ibn Kharashah, Sahl ibn Hunayf, and al-Harith ibn al-Simmah. He said to them: If you wish, you may divide among the Emigrants from your wealth and your homes and share with them in this spoil; and if you wish, your homes and wealth will remain yours and nothing of the spoil will be divided for you. The Helpers said: Rather, we will divide for them from our wealth and our homes, and we will prefer them with the spoil and not share it with them; so this verse was revealed." This is explicit that the words of the Exalted: ﴿And those who had settled﴾ ... etc. are a resumptive statement, not conjoined to the poor or the Emigrants. Yes, it is permissible to conjoin it to "those" (ulaika), since that only requires the Helpers' partnership with the Emigrants in truthfulness, not in the fay'; then the words of the Exalted: ﴿They love﴾ and what is conjoined to it are a resumptive statement confirming their truthfulness, or a circumstantial phrase (hal) from the pronoun of "tabawwu'u."

﴿And whoever is protected from the stinginess (shuhh) of his soul﴾: shuhh, with a damma or a kasra, and it has also been read with them: avarice. Its attribution to the soul is because it is an innate disposition in it that calls for greed to withhold, which is miserliness. That is: whoever is protected, by God's granting success, from its stinginess, so that he opposes it in what dominates it of love of wealth and hatred of spending.

﴿Those﴾ is a pointing to "whoever" in view of its general meaning, which encompasses those mentioned in a preliminary way.

﴿they are the successful﴾: those who attain every desired thing and are saved from every disliked thing. The clause is a parenthetical interjection (i'tiraD) coming to praise the Helpers and commend them. It has been read "yuwaqq" with the doubled letter.

The Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 59, verse 10:

﴿And those who came after them⁠﴾ are those who emigrated after Islam had become strong, or the Successors who follow them in goodness, and they are the believers after both groups until the Day of Resurrection. For this reason it has been said that the verse has encompassed all the believers. In any case, the relative pronoun (al-mawsul) is the subject (mubtada'), and its predicate (khabar) is ﴿they say﴾ ...etc. The sentence is brought to praise them for their love toward those who preceded them among the believers, and their observance of the rights of brotherhood in religion and of precedence in faith, just as "ma" (in "ma 'utifat 'alayhi") is conjoined to it from the preceding sentence, which praises the Helpers; that is, they supplicate for them.

﴿Our Lord, forgive us and our brothers⁠﴾ That is, in the religion, which is more honorable and more noble in their sight than lineage.

﴿who preceded us in faith⁠﴾ They describe them thus, acknowledging their virtue.

﴿And do not place in our hearts any rancor⁠﴾ It is also read as "ghimran," and both mean resentment.

﴿toward those who believe⁠﴾ in general.

﴿Our Lord, You are indeed Compassionate and Merciful⁠﴾ That is, You are exceedingly full of tenderness and mercy, so You are worthy to answer our supplication.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 59, verse 11:

﴿Have you not considered those who played the hypocrite?﴾ This is a narration of what passed between the disbelievers and the hypocrites of false statements and corrupt conditions, and an expression of wonder at them, after the narration of the fine conditions and statements of the believers across their different ranks. The address is to the Messenger of God (ﷺ), or to everyone who has a share of being addressed. His words, exalted is He, ﴿they say﴾ ... etc., are a resumptive clause (isti'naf) explaining the object of wonder. The use of the present tense (al-mudari') is to indicate the continuity of their saying, or to bring its image vividly before the mind. The lam in His words, exalted is He, ﴿to their brothers who disbelieved among the People of the Book﴾ is the lam of communication (lam al-tabligh), and by their "brotherhood" is meant either their agreement in disbelief or their friendship and alliance. The lam in His words, exalted is He, ﴿If you are expelled﴾ means: from your homes by force, and it is a lam preparing for an oath (lam al-muwatti'a lil-qasam). His words, exalted is He, ﴿we will surely go out with you﴾ are the answer to the oath, meaning: by God, if you are expelled, we will certainly go out with you, absolutely, and we will surely accompany you wherever you go.

﴿And we will not obey anyone against you﴾ meaning: concerning your affair.

﴿Anyone﴾ who would prevent us from going out with you.

﴿Ever﴾ even if time is prolonged. It has been said that it means: we will not obey (anyone) concerning your fighting or abandonment, but this is not the case, because the assumption of fighting is still awaited, and because their promise to them under that assumption is not merely a non-obedience to those who call them to fight against them, but rather their support against him, as His words, exalted is He, indicate: ﴿And if you are fought, we will surely support you﴾, meaning: we will surely aid you against your enemy. Moreover, their calling them to abandon the Jews is something that could not issue from the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and the Muslims, so that they could claim non-obedience to them in it; this is because, had it been so, it would have been at the time of their readiness to support them and manifest their disbelief. There is no doubt that what he (peace be upon him) would do at that time is to kill them, not to call them to abandon their support. As for going out with them, it is not at this level of manifesting disbelief, since it is possible for them to claim that their going out with them was due to the worldly friendship between them, not for agreement in religion.

﴿And God testifies that they are surely liars﴾ in their promises, which were emphasized with false oaths.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 59, verse 12:

And His saying, ﴿Should they be expelled, they will not go out with them﴾ ... etc., is a refutation of each one of their statements in detail, after refuting them all in summary.

﴿And should they be fought, they will not help them﴾ — and the matter was so: Ibn Ubayy and his companions sent word to the Banu al-Nadir of this secretly, then they broke their promise to them. In this there is a clear proof of the truth of prophethood and of the miraculous nature (i'jaz) of the Qur'an.

﴿And should they help them﴾ — on the assumption and supposition.

﴿They will surely turn their backs﴾ — in flight.

﴿Then they will not be helped﴾ — i.e., the hypocrites after that, meaning: Allah will destroy them, and their hypocrisy will not benefit them because their disbelief has become manifest; or, the Jews will be defeated, then the support of the hypocrites will not benefit them.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 59, verse 13:

﴿Indeed, you are more fearsome﴾ That is: more inspiring of dread (ma'rubiyyah), taking it as a verbal noun (masdar) derived from the passive form (al-mabni li-l-maf'ul).

﴿in their breasts than Allah﴾ That is: their dread of you in secret is greater than the dread of Allah that they display to you, for they used to claim among themselves a great dread of Allah, exalted is He.

﴿That﴾ That is: what has been mentioned, namely that their dread of you is greater than the dread of Allah.

﴿is because﴾ on account of the fact that.

﴿they are a people who do not comprehend﴾ That is: [who do not comprehend] anything, until they know the greatness of Allah, exalted is He, and so fear Him with the fear that is due to Him.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 59, verse 14:

﴿They will not fight you all together⦆ — that is, the Jews and the hypocrites; the meaning is: they are not able to fight you.

﴿All together﴾ — that is, gathered and united in one place out of the places.

﴿Except in fortified towns﴾ — fortified with barricades (durub) and trenches (khandaq).

﴿Or from behind walls﴾ — without coming out to you in the open and meeting you in single combat, because of the extremity of their dread. It is read "judr" (with the vowel lightened) and read "jidar," and with the fatha of the dal inclined (imalah), and "jadr" and "judar," and they all mean the wall (al-jidar).

﴿Their violence among themselves is severe﴾ — a resumptive statement brought to clarify that what has been mentioned of their dread is not due to weakness and cowardice within themselves, for their violence toward their peers is severe; rather, their weakness and cowardice are in relation to you, because of the terror God Most High has cast into their hearts.

﴿You think them to be together﴾ — gathered and united.

﴿But their hearts are divided﴾ — scattered, with no harmony between them.

﴿That is because they﴾ — that is, the scattering of their hearts that has been mentioned is due to the fact that they

﴿are a people who do not reason﴾ — that is, they do not reason about anything until they recognize the truth and follow it, and their hearts are at peace with it, and their word is unified, and they shoot from one bow; so they fall into the wilderness of error, and their hearts are scattered according to the scattering of its paths and the dispersal of its branches. As for what has been said, that the meaning is: they do not reason that the scattering of hearts weakens their strength, it is far from being sound.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 59, verse 15:

And His saying, ﴿Like those before them﴾ is the predicate of an omitted subject, its estimate being "their example" (mathaluhum), i.e., the example of those mentioned from among the Jews and the hypocrites is like the example of the people of Badr, or the Banu Qaynuqa' according to what has been said, that they were expelled before the Banu al-Nadir.

﴿Recently﴾ means in a near time. Its being in the accusative is by an estimate like this one, as in "the occurrence of the example of ..., etc." ﴿They tasted the evil of their affair﴾ means the evil outcome of their disbelief in this world.

﴿And for them﴾ in the Hereafter.

﴿Is a painful punishment﴾ whose extent cannot be measured. The meaning is: the state of these people is like the state of those in this world and the Hereafter, but not in the sense that the state of all of them is like their state; rather, the state of some of them, who are the Jews, is like that, while the state of the hypocrites is what He has expressed.

(p-232) His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Like the example of Satan, when he says to man, "Disbelieve." But when he disbelieves, he says, "Indeed, I am free of you; indeed, I fear Allah, Lord of the worlds."﴾

﴿Like the example of Satan﴾: this is a second predicate (khabar thani) for an implied subject (mubtada' muqaddar), clarifying their condition and including another condition relating to the Jews, namely their being deceived by the hypocrites' promise at first and their disappointment in the end. In the noble composition, both predicates are attributed to the implied noun that is annexed to the pronoun of the two groups, without specifying precisely to which it is attributed, relying on the listener's understanding that he will match each of the two examples with what resembles it. It is as if it were said: the example of the Jews in the descent of punishment upon them is like the example of those before them... etc., and the example of the hypocrites in their inciting them to fight, as was reported about them, is like the example of Satan.

﴿When he says to man, "Disbelieve."﴾ That is, he incited him to disbelief, as one who commands incites the one commanded to the thing commanded.

﴿But when he disbelieves, he says, "Indeed, I am free of you."﴾ It has been recited as "Anā barī'un minka" (I am free of you). If by "man" is meant the species, then this disavowal by Satan will take place on the Day of Resurrection, as His saying, may He be exalted, indicates: ﴿Indeed, I fear Allah, Lord of the worlds.﴾ If by "man" is meant Abu Jahl, then His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿Disbelieve﴾ is an expression for the statement of Iblis on the day of Badr: ﴿No one among the people can overcome you today, and indeed I am a protector for you.﴾ And his disavowal is his saying on that day: ﴿Indeed, I am free of you. Indeed, I see what you do not see. Indeed, I fear Allah﴾ — the verse.

﴿So the end of both of them was﴾ is in the accusative (nasb), as the predicate (khabar) of kāna (a verb of being, "was") and its subject (ism), with ʿāqibatahumā as the predicate.

﴿that they are in the Fire﴾ It has also been recited in the reverse order. It has already been mentioned that the first reading is clearer.

﴿abiding therein﴾ It has also been recited as "khālidāni fīhā" (abiding, in the dual nominative), with that being the predicate of inna (the emphatic particle "indeed"). In that case "fī al-nār" (in the Fire) is redundant (laghw).

﴿and that is the recompense of the wrongdoers﴾ That is, abiding in the Fire is the recompense of the wrongdoers in general, not of these particular people alone.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (*Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim*) on surah 59, verse 18:

﴿O you who have believed, fear Allah﴾, that is: in everything you do and everything you leave undone.

﴿And let every soul look to what it has put forward for tomorrow﴾, that is: what deeds it has sent ahead for the Day of Resurrection. He expressed it this way because it is near, or because the worldly life is like a day and the Hereafter is its tomorrow. Its indefiniteness (*tankir*) is for magnifying and terrifying it, as if it were said: "for a tomorrow whose true nature is not known because of its great immensity." As for the indefiniteness of ﴿soul﴾, it is for the independence of each soul that looks at what it has sent ahead for that awesome Day, as if it were said: "let one single soul look at that."

﴿And fear Allah﴾: it is a repetition for emphasis, or the first refers to performing the obligations, as what follows of the command to act indicates, and this refers to abandoning the prohibited acts, as the warning indicates in His words, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, Allah is Acquainted with what you do﴾, that is: of acts of disobedience.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 59, verse 19:

﴿And do not be like those who forgot Allah﴾. That is: they forgot His rights and did not give Him His due measure, and did not observe the obligations of His commands and prohibitions as they should have been observed.

﴿So He caused them to forget themselves﴾ as a consequence of that.

﴿Themselves﴾, that is: He made them forgetful of them, so that they did not hear what would benefit them and did not do what would save them; or it means He showed them, on the Day of Resurrection, such terrors that they made them forget themselves.

﴿Those﴾ (p-233) ﴿they are﴾.

﴿The defiantly disobedient﴾, those who are complete in defiant disobedience (fusuq).

﴿Not equal are the companions of the Fire,﴾ those who forgot God, the Exalted, and so became deserving of eternal abiding in the Fire.

﴿and the companions of the Garden,﴾ those who were mindful of God and so became deserving of eternal abiding in the Garden. The mention of the companions of the Fire first is perhaps to signal from the outset that the restriction (qasr) indicated by the non-equality lies on their side, not on the side of their counterparts. The concept of non-equality between two things that differ in excess and deficiency may be considered in terms of the excess of the one who has more, but what comes first to mind is considering it in terms of the deficiency of the one who has less. Accordingly is God's statement: "Are the blind and the seeing equal?" and "Or are the darknesses and the light equal?" and other such instances. As for God's statement, ﴿Are those who know and those who do not know equal?﴾, the mention of the superior party first there may be because its attribute is an acquired disposition (malakah) relative to the attribute of the inferior party, and privations (a'dam) are preceded by their corresponding dispositions. There is no indication in this noble verse that a Muslim may not retaliate against an unbeliever, or that unbelievers may not seize the wealth of Muslims by force, because what is intended is non-equality in the matter of the Hereafter, as is indicated by the expression of the two groups as the companionship of the Fire and the companionship of the Garden. Likewise is God's statement: ﴿The companions of the Garden are the triumphant.﴾ It is a resumptive clause (istiʾnaf) explaining the manner of the non-equality between the two groups, that is: they are the ones who attain every desired thing and are saved from every disliked thing.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 59, verse 21:

﴿Had We sent down this Qur'an﴾ (the one of great standing, containing the various kinds of awe-striking admonitions).

﴿upon a mountain﴾ of the mountains.

﴿you would have seen it﴾ — despite it being a sign of hardness and of being unaffected by whatever strikes it.

﴿humbled, split asunder out of the fear of God﴾ — that is, cracked apart out of it. It is also read as "muṣaddaʿan" with idgham (assimilation of the letters). This is a parable and an imaginative depiction of the exalted status of the Qur'an and the strength of the influence of the admonitions within it, as expressed by His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And these parables We set forth for the people, that perhaps they may reflect﴾. It is intended as a rebuke to the human being for the hardness of his heart, his lack of humility when reciting it, and his scant reflection upon it.

**He is Allah, other than whom there is no deity** (alone).

﴿Knower of the unseen and the witnessed﴾. That is: what is hidden from the senses, namely the holy substances (*al-jawahir al-qudsiyyah*, immaterial substances) and their states, and what is present to Him of physical bodies (*ajram*) and their accidents (*a'rad*, accidents). The unseen is placed before the witnessed because of its precedence in existence and because eternal knowledge relates to it first. Alternatively, it refers to the non-existent and the existent, or to the secret and the open.

﴿He is the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful﴾.

﴿He is Allah, other than whom there is no deity but Him﴾ is repeated to highlight the importance of the matter of tawhid (divine oneness).

﴿The King, the Holy﴾: the one who is supremely free from anything that would entail deficiency. It is also read with a fatha (al-Qaddus), and this is a dialectal form of the same word.

﴿The Peace﴾: the one who is free from every deficiency and defect. It is a verbal noun (masdar) used as an attribute for emphasis.

﴿The Giver of Security﴾: the one who bestows safety. It is also read with a fatha (al-Mu'manu), meaning "the one through whom security is attained," with the preposition omitted.

﴿The Guardian﴾: the watchful one who protects everything. It is a mufay'il form (mufay'il, a morphological pattern) derived from amn (security), with its hamza (glottal stop letter) changed to a haa.

﴿The Almighty﴾: the Victorious.

﴿The Compeller﴾: the one who compelled His creation to what He willed, or who set their affairs right, i.e., repaired them.

﴿The Majestic﴾: the one who is exalted above everything that would entail need or deficiency, or the one who is most perfect in greatness and magnificence.

﴿Glory be to Allah above what they associate with Him﴾: a declaration of His exaltation above what they associate with Him, or above their associating partners with Him, following the enumeration of His attributes, none of which can be shared by anything whatsoever with Him, Exalted is He.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 59, verse 24:

﴿He is Allah, the Creator (al-Khaliq)﴾ who determines things according to the requirements of His wisdom.

﴿The Originator (al-Bari')﴾ who brings them into existence free from disparity; and it is said: the One who distinguishes some of them from others by their different forms.

﴿The Fashioner (al-Musawwir)﴾ who brings into existence their forms and modes as He wills.

﴿To Him belong the Most Beautiful Names (al-Asma' al-Husna)﴾ because they indicate meanings that are good.

﴿Whatever is in the heavens and the earth glorifies Him﴾ speaks of His exaltedness above all deficiencies, a manifest exaltation.

﴿And He is the Mighty (al-'Aziz), the Wise (al-Hakim)﴾ who encompasses all perfections in their entirety, for they, despite their multiplicity and diversity, all return to perfection in power and knowledge.

From the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whoever recites Surat al-Hashr, Allah will forgive him what he has previously done of his sins and what he has later done."
